title: After Flipping Blue, a California City Syncs Up Local Elections with High-Turnout Contests
author: Pascal Sabino
content:
The city of Whittier, just east of Los Angeles, elected its first Latino-
majority city council this spring after [a slate of Democratic candidates
swept local elections](https://boltsmag.org/california-immigrant-organizing-
and-elections-in-whittier/). It was a major upset not only because a longtime
mayor and councilors lost in a landslide, but also because the results defied
the city’s oddly-timed spring elections; historically, that timing has
dampened turnout and helped more conservative and largely white politicians
remain in office.

Now, voters have approved a measure to reschedule Whittier’s local elections
so they align with higher-turnout state and federal contests in the fall.
Advocates say the change will ensure city officials are chosen by a larger and
more diverse electorate than in the past, and help Whittier’s government
better represent the people who live there.

The measure was placed on the ballot by the new councilors elected in March,
fulfilling a core campaign promise. “Off-cycle elections are a form of voter
suppression,” James Becerra, the victorious candidate for mayor, told _Bolts_
this spring. Becerra and his allies
[proposed](https://file.lacounty.gov/SDSInter/bos/supdocs/219020.pdf)
scheduling future local elections in November of even-numbered years, and
their reform passed on Nov. 3 by an overwhelming margin, 80 percent to 20
percent.

“This is going to guarantee that we have a city council that represents what
the city of Whittier looks like, in terms of the diversity we have in the
city,” said Angie Medina, the leader of a local Latino community organization
and a longtime advocate for changing the timing of elections in Whittier.
“This was the number one factor in terms of getting fair elections and
ensuring a high voter turnout.”

“It's nice to see this is going to be the future for the city of Whittier,”
said Medina.

Once a bastion of conservatism best known as Richard Nixon’s hometown,
Whittier has been predominantly Latino for decades, and it now reliably votes
blue in federal and state elections. But that pattern hadn’t held true for
local elections, as [_Bolts_ reported in May](https://boltsmag.org/california-
immigrant-organizing-and-elections-in-whittier/); until this year few Latinos
had been elected to office since the 1990s.

Research has shown that off-cycle elections reduce turnout among groups who
tend to be under-represented at the polls, including renters, young people,
and voters of color.

According to Luis Reyes, who led the campaign urging voters to approve the
change to November elections, many Whittier residents weren’t tuned in to
local politics until recent years. Few people were engaged in the springtime
elections, and not many people were aware of the political beliefs of their
elected officials.

The surge in immigration enforcement last year changed that dynamic, according
to Reyes. Whittier residents [gathered to protest ICE
raids](https://lapublicpress.org/2025/06/whittier-la-ice-raids-protest/) in
the region and they expressed anger that local officials [were
not](https://lapublicpress.org/2025/06/whittier-la-ice-raids-protest/) doing
more to protect their constituents from the federal agents showing up at local
car washes and city buildings. “We had a mayor that was there for 20 years
that never really showed his partisanship,” said Reyes. “But when people
needed help, his philosophy and his viewpoints came out, and it was definitely
not in line with the majority of community members.”

Community groups like the Whittier Latino Coalition have advocated for over a
decade for changing local election dates to coincide with higher-profile
races. In 2013, a group of residents affiliated with the coalition [sued the
city, alleging voter suppression](https://www.latimes.com/local/political/la-
me-pc-whittier-elections-system-20130814-story.html), including a claim that
the low-turnout April date weakened the power of Latino voters. They dropped
the lawsuit after the city agreed to other reforms—abandoning its at-large
system and creating anchoring districts around predominantly Latino
neighborhoods—but what remained unchanged was the election date in the spring.

Whittier briefly synced up its elections with California’s presidential
primaries in 2020 to comply with the California Voter Participation Rights
Act, a reform that required cities to align their local elections with a state
contest if turnout fell below a certain threshold.

As a result, turnout in the 2020 mayoral race surged to 44 percent. In
Whittier’s previous mayoral election in the spring of 2018, it had only
reached 18 percent.

But a state court the following year
[exempted](https://law.justia.com/cases/california/court-of-
appeal/2020/b294016.html) some cities from that law, and Whittier’s city
council chose to return local elections to the spring. Voter participation
plummeted.

“It had been really frustrating to see the city change the date back to
spring,” Medina told _Bolts._ “There was no real reason to do it unless you
are trying to suppress voters.”

Becerra and the candidates who ran alongside him for city council, Vicky
Santana and Aida Macedo, all promised on the campaign trail to support moving
local elections to November. Shortly after their sweep, the council—including
its sole remaining conservative member, Cathy Warner—unanimously approved a
charter amendment to change the date of local elections, placing it on the
November ballot.

Now that voters have approved it, the measure will first go into effect in
2028.

![](https://boltsmag.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/Macedo.jpg)Aida Macedo, a
new city councilor in Whittier, supported changing the timing of local
elections. (Photo from Pascal Sabino/Bolts)

Joe Vinatieri, the former mayor who lost to Becerra in April, posted about his
opposition to the measure on social media,
[saying](https://www.facebook.com/Joev4whittier/posts/ive-had-a-number-of-
people-ask-for-my-thoughts-on-whittier-ballot-measures-el-
te/1796754469122385/) that moving local elections to the fall would drown out
local issues. “There are over 55 different propositions, judges, candidates,
measures, etc. to find my way through,” he wrote about his November ballot.
“When Whittier has its own stand alone election in April, there is none of
this non-Whittier ‘clutter’ on the ballot.” (Vinatieri did not reply to a
request for comment for this story.)

But the new councilors say the measure’s success at the polls shows residents
want it to be easier to engage in politics.

“People in Whittier want to be brought into local policy and local decision
making,” Macedo told _Bolts_. “I think they see that if they don’t know when
their election is, and if there’s no uniformity with state elections, then
they know that they’re being left out.”

* * *

Whittier joins many other cities that have made a similar change as a way to
boost participation, including the neighboring metropolis of Los Angeles,
where voters approved this change in
[2015](https://ballotpedia.org/City_of_Los_Angeles_New_City_Election_Dates_and_Schedules_Charter_Amendment,_Measure_1_\(March_2015\)).

[San Francisco, Boulder](https://boltsmag.org/even-year-local-elections/), and
[Phoenix](https://www.kjzz.org/2020-10-07/content-1624344-its-critical-
election-phoenix-mayor-4-city-council-seats) have also adjusted their
schedules recently, resulting in skyrocketing turnout for local contests. In a
rare major defeat for proponents of this change, New York City voters last
year [refused to reschedule](https://boltsmag.org/new-york-city-even-year-
local-elections/) their municipal elections.

This fall, voters in many places signaled their preference for elections to
align. In Austin, they approved a
[measure](https://ballotpedia.org/Austin,_Texas,_Proposition_G,_Initiative_Elections_Charter_Amendment_\(November_2026\))
that requires citizen initiatives to go on the ballot in November of even-
numbered years. In New Mexico, voters repealed a [state
rule](https://nmindepth.com/2026/a-voting-relic-on-the-ballot/) that stopped
school board elections from sharing a ballot with partisan state races.

Voters in the Florida city of North Miami Beach, meanwhile, rejected a
proposal that would have moved their local elections in the opposite
direction, from November to May.

The North Miami Beach commissioners who backed the measure, called Referendum
4, made a similar case to Vinatieri’s, that local issues get lost in the
shuffle when city elections fall on the same date as big-ticket races like
U.S. Senate or governor. If the city had its own dedicated election, they
said, the voters who participated would be more knowledgeable, as opposed to
treating downballot races as an afterthought.

Commissioner Fortuna Smukler said in a public meeting in July that "the people
who vote in May will be knowledgeable," whereas voters in November "may just
pick a name because they are there." (Smukler did not respond to _Bolts_ ’
request for an interview, nor did other commissioners who supported the
measure.)

North Miami Beach is home to one of the largest Haitian-American communities
in the country, and Haitian-Americans politicians [have gained
influence](https://www.miamiherald.com/news/local/community/miami-dade/north-
miami/article250141274.html) locally, and helped secure North Miami Beach’s
first, short-lived majority-Black commission from 2020 to 2022. Since then,
policy [disagreements among city
leadership](https://www.miamitimesonline.com/news/local/a-north-miami-beach-
in-turmoil/article_2907554c-cda3-11ed-98ba-f7374d4be859.html) have often
fallen along racial lines.

Mayor Michael Joseph, who is Haitian-American, opposed the proposal to move
local elections to the spring. He voted against placing it on the ballot, as
did the two other Black members on the seven-member commission.

“Moving municipal elections to the spring could result in fewer residents
having a voice in decisions that directly affect their communities,” Joseph
told _Bolts_. “We should be looking for ways to encourage more participation,
not creating additional barriers to it.”

The measure lost by 40 percentage points.

* * *

In Whittier, besides rescheduling elections, the council’s new members
proposed imposing 12-year term limits on city officials, and voters approved
that reform as well. The council members also say they’re serious about
shoring up protections against ICE, the issue that helped sweep them into
office in the first place.

In June, when ICE vehicles showed up near the library, a hub for community
programs like one that offers free lunches to kids over the summer, the new
mayor showed up to [question the
agents](https://www.youtube.com/shorts/4mc4veYE1D8) inside and press them to
identify themselves. _The Whittier Daily News_
[reports](https://www.whittierdailynews.com/2026/06/10/on-1-year-anniversary-
of-ice-raids-agents-return-to-whittier-this-time-the-new-mayor-confronts-
them/) that the vehicles ended up leaving without making arrests.

Federal immigration officials released a statement
[saying](https://www.whittierdailynews.com/2026/06/11/federal-officials-say-
whittier-mayors-encounter-with-ice-agent-was-interference-with-immigration-
probe/) Becerra “made his community less safe” by confronting ICE agents.

![](https://boltsmag.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/11/WhittierBecerra-e1795476740980.jpg)Whittier Mayor
James Becerra confronts ICE agents parked in front of the local public library
in June 2026, as seen in the screenshot of a video recorded by Brenda
Castillo. (Video via Castillo)

Macedo, who joined Becerra near the library that day, says the incident helped
her realize that the city had no formal plans in place to alert participants
who might be at the library or on the way there about federal agent presence.

In June, Macedo and other councilors
[ordered](https://www.whittier360newsnetwork.com/post/breaking-news-whittier-
council-votes-5-0-to-draft-ice-response-protocol-after-special-meeting-draws)
the development of protocols to instruct city workers on how to respond to ICE
sightings, such as sending warnings to people who are participating in library
programs. Macedo says __it was important for her to figure out how a city
council could respond to the federal government, telling _Bolts_ , “We know
all the things we cannot do, but what _can_ we do?”

“I think it was really frustrating to the residents to see what was happening
in our city and for there not be even any acknowledgement,” Macedo said. “I
think just even acknowledging that we cared and that we wanted to do something
to protect our residents was the change that a lot of residents wanted.”
